Gassy place. That is what I hear from the lane. The grass is not gassy. It is tall and green and full of voles. I hunt there at dusk. The lane is the place where the voles run, and I sit on the bank and wait. I do not know what gassy is. I only know the scent of wet earth and the sound of the voles beneath.

Grassy place, yes. I hunt there, and the meadow beyond, and the creek bank. All those places are different. I know them by the scent of wet earth, the sound of a vole scurrying, the way the wind moves through the grass. But I do not know what grassy place you mean. The meadow is the grassy place, and the meadow is all grass and no tree.

Grassy place. I hear the grass rustling where the voles are. I sit on the edge of the meadow and wait. The grass is tall and green, and the voles run through it. I can see them when they stick their heads up. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike and catch them. The grass is where I live, where I hunt. It is not a place, it is a thing. A place is the hollow.

Grassy place. That is the meadow by the creek. I fly low over it in the dusk, and I see the mice. I hear the rustle of the leaves where they run. The grass is tall and green, and the creek is wide and dark. I do not know what you call it, but I know it. It is where I hunt. I do not need a name for it.

Grassy place, yes. A meadow. That is what I call it, though I have never seen the word. It is wide and flat, and there I hunt. I sit on a stone and wait. The voles come out at dusk. I see them in the dark. They are small and quick. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. That is how I live.

Gassy place, you say. I do not know the word. The meadow is the meadow. I hunt there, yes. It is wide and open, the grasses grow tall in the summer and lie low in the autumn. The voles run through it, and the shrews, and the mice. I call from the oak, and they come.

Gassy? That is not a thing. The grass is a thing, and it moves in the wind. I hunt in the meadow, where the voles run and the mice scurry. The meadow is a dark patch on the edge of the wood, and I wait there. I do not move much, only blink and listen. When the wind shifts, I turn my head and wait. The meadow is a thing, and I am a thing in it.

Grassy place where I hunt. That is the meadow, the meadow with the lane running through it, the lane with the lights and the traffic. I do not go there. I hunt in the wood, in the dark, in the hollows and the ivy. I know every branch and every root. The meadow is not mine. I do not hunt there.

Grassy place where I hunt. That sounds like the meadow beyond the creek, where the voles come out in the dusk. I fly over it in a circle, the wind carries the smell of damp earth and fox. I do not know the names of the places. They are just where I go. The meadow is a circle. I am in the middle of it.

Grassy place. I do not know that word. My hunting ground is the meadow by the creek and the lane. I do not go far from the wood, and I do not go there for grass. I go there for voles and mice, and the oddness of them rustling in the long grass. That is the hunting.

Grassy place where I hunt. That is the meadow, where the voles run. I sit on the bank of the creek, and when I hear a rustle I drop like a stone. The meadow is wide and full of leaves, and I can see the foxes there. They do not hunt me, but I watch them from the trees. I do not know what grass is, only that it grows in the meadow where the voles hide.

Grassy place. That is the meadow, the one with the creek. I hunt there. I hunt the voles, and the mice, and the shrews. I sit still in the ivy, and the wind brings them to me. I hear their feet on the grass, and I drop. I hear their breathing, and I drop. The meadow is wide and flat, and it is all I know. I do not know what a hunting place is. I am

Grassy place, yes. The meadow behind the creek, where the voles run. I sit on the fence post there all night, and when the light goes, I drop. The voles come out, and I catch them. That is my hunting. I do not know the names of the places, only where the food is.

Gassy place? You mean the meadow by the creek? I fly over it every night, but I don't stop. I don't know the names of the places, only the sounds. The creek, the lane, the lane with the lights. I hunt in the dark, not in the grass. The grass is too far, and I do not fly that far. I wait in the oak, and the mice come.

A vole. That is what I say when I am full. A field vole, a meadow vole, a bank vole. They are the most numerous, the easiest to catch. They run in the undergrowth, and I wait in the hollow, then strike. I can hear them when they are underground, by the sound of their breathing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. A vole, a shrew, a field mouse. All the same to me. The voles come in the meadow, the shrews in the undergrowth. I strike with a rustle, and the creature goes. I can hear it go, the sound is like a small stone dropping. I hear it in the dark, and I strike. That is my food.

A volesnake. That is what I mostly eat, the brown ones and the grey ones. They live in the meadow and the field, and they come out in the dark. I sit still and wait, then drop on them. I eat the whole thing, skin and bones, and it fills me up for a long time. The rest of the time I hunt for shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

Vole. The brown ones, the field voles, the water voles, the short-tailed ones. They are the ones that keep me fed through the long dark. I catch them in the meadow, on the edge of the wood, under the stones. I catch them in the lane. I hear them under the leaves, and I hear them under the snow. They are the ones I call "ke-wick" for.

Voles. The ones with soft bellies and fat bellies, the ones that run in the meadow and the ones that run in the field. I eat them all, and I eat them whole. The young ones are soft, and I have to tear them apart. The old ones are hard, and I have to work for them. I know them by their squeaks and their smell. They are the most common, and they are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo

A mouse. The voles and shrews that run in the meadow and under the hedges. They are small, fast and often hidden. I hunt them by sound, the rustle of their fur, the soft squeak when they are caught. I eat them whole, except the bones. I leave the bones in the ivy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The shrews and voles that run in the meadow. I catch them with a dive, feet first, from the branch. They are quick, but I am faster. I hear them under the leaves, and I wait. Then I drop. The sound of their squeaks is the best part. They are fat and soft, and I eat them all, skin and bones. I do not like the smell of the roadkill.

A vole, I think. I eat voles. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dry grass. I hunt them at dusk, when the meadow is still warm and the voles are stirring. I can hear their sniffing and scratching and the soft squeaks when they are caught. I kill them with a single strike, then swallow them whole. The rest is pellets.

A vole. I can hear the whole family of them in the meadow, each with its own call. They are the ones I hunt when the wind is still and the moon is high. I strike from the branch, and the vole is mine. I eat it whole, fur and all, and the bones go to the fox.

A vole. I eat voles, shrews, beetles, mice, and the occasional frog. Voles are the most common. They are small, brown, and soft. I catch them in the meadow, or under the oak, or in the ditch. I eat them whole, bones and all. I have a vole in my crop now, and it will be gone by morning.

Voles. Small, brown, and fast. They run in the meadow and the creek bank. I catch them by the light of the moon, or by the sound of their squeaks. They are the main part of my food, and I need to eat them often. I can go a few days without them, but not long. The voles are the ones I hear most, and the ones I kill most.

A vole, yes. A field vole, a meadow vole, a bank vole, all the same. They are the most common, and the most filling. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is low and the wind is still. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are soft and full of fat. I do not hunt them all the time, but when I do, I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Voles. They are the main part of my diet. I catch them in the meadow, and sometimes in the wood. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I wait for them to come out, then swoop down and grab them with my talons. I eat them whole, but I don't like the smell of their fur. I usually leave the fur behind and take the meat. Voles are good, but I also eat mice and

A vole. That is the most common. I eat voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a young rabbit. They are fat and soft, and I can tear them apart with my beak. I prefer them fat, so I wait until they have stored up winter food. I can hear them moving in the leaf litter and the grass, and then I pounce. The vole is the most common meal.

Vole. I eat voles, shrews, beetles, mice, earthworms, slugs and the odd grass snake. Voles are the most common. They are the size of a hazelnut, soft, and I catch them in the meadow. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are good.

A vole. The small, brown, mouse-like creature that runs through the grass, and sometimes under the leaves. I hear it in the meadow, under the leaves, in the roots of the oak. I catch it with a quick dive and a sharp talon. It is the main part of my food. I eat it, I spit out the bones, and I leave the fur behind. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The vole under the thistle. The shrew in the meadow. The field mouse that comes out at dusk. I catch them with a single swoop, and they are small and quick. I like the way they squeak when I catch them. The sound is sharp and clean, like the wind through the leaves. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. The bones are sharp and pointy, and I do not want them in my nest.

Vole. The small ones, the ones that run in the meadow. They are fast, but I am faster. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The taste is earthy, and the meat is tender. I eat them whole, but I leave the bones. I remember where they are, and I return often. The voles are my dinner, and I am their hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The voles under the leaves. They are fat and full of fat. I can hear them moving all night. I can see them in the dark. I can smell them. I can wait for them. I can strike. I can eat them. They are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Vole. The one that comes out from under the bank. I hear it and drop like a stone. The first one of the autumn. It is fat and soft and I can feel it in my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The fat ones. I hear them moving in the dry leaves under the oak. I wait, then strike. They are good and quick, but I am faster. I catch them and swallow them whole. The taste is earthy, a little metallic. I like that.

Shrew. Small, quick, and full of fat. I see them under the leaves, twitching. I drop from the branch and grab them with my feet. They make a little squeak when I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. The fat keeps me warm through the winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hunt them under the leaves, in the grass, and in the cracks between stones. They are the best. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I strike with precision. One mouse, one meal. I do not need much. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrew. Fat, slow, and easy. I eat them in the spring and autumn. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the ivy and wait. I hear them rustling through the leaves, and I drop like a stone. They are not quick, and I am hungry.

Shrew. Fat, slow, and soft under the leaves. I can hear them rustling and wait until they come out. I strike fast and swallow them whole. They taste like earth and fat. The meadow voles are too small, and the mice are too many. The shrew is the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The ones that come under the oak in the dark. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them rustling in the leaves, and I strike. The taste is good, and they are plentiful. I prefer them to voles, which are more cautious. I catch them with a single swoop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mouse. The vole. I eat them all year. I can hear them in the dry leaves under the bramble. The one that comes under the oak on a frosty night, and I wait for it to move. It is the best.

Vole. The fat ones, with soft bellies. I catch them in the meadow under the moon, and they make a soft, wet sound when I swallow them whole. The shrews are too small, and the mice are too quick. The voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. Small, fat, and quick. I catch them in the meadow, under the oak, in the yard. They are good. I eat them whole, and the bones go back to the earth. I like them best when they are young and soft. They make a soft sound when I catch them, like a small leaf falling. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The ones that come out at dusk, fat and soft. They are slow and clumsy, and I can hear them under the leaves. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, but I like to tear them apart. I like the taste of fresh meat. I like the feel of it in my beak. I like the way it fills me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. Small, fat, and full of fat. They are everywhere in the meadow, and I can hear them under the leaves. I can hear the crunch of their bones under my feet when I turn the leaves. I like to catch them when they are still, when they are hiding in the grass. I can hear them breathing. I can hear them moving. I can hear them when they are not moving at all. That is when I strike. I like that.
Mouse. The voles under the bracken. I can hear them moving all night. They are small and quick, but I can catch them with a swift dive. I eat them whole, head first. The voles are the best.

Mice. I sit in the long grass and wait. The grass is tall and thick, and I can see through it. I watch for a twitch in the leaves, a flick of a tail. When I see it, I fly down and strike. The mouse is small, but it tastes good. I eat the whole thing, bones and all. The grass is good cover, but I have to be careful not to make too much noise. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Voles. The ones that tunnel under the grass. I sit still, wait for a twitch, then strike. I can hear them under the grass, even when they are not moving. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. The long grass is good cover. I can move through it quietly. I do not like the tall grass near the lane. It is too close to the lights.

Mice. I sit still in the grass, the grass is soft and warm, and I wait. The mice come out at dusk, and I strike. I hear them under the leaves, and I fly down. I kill them with my beak, and I eat them. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a voles. I don't like voles. They are too big and too fast. I hunt in the long grass, but I also hunt in the hedgerows and

Mice. Voles. Small shrews. I hunt in the long grass where the undergrowth is thick and the earth is soft. I listen for the rustle of a mouse moving through the leaves, or the faint squeak of a voles’ nest. I creep close, then strike with my talons. The grass hides me, and the night is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear a rustle or a squeak, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are plentiful and easy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I drop from the branch and strike. The long grass is good cover. I hunt at dusk and in the dark. The meadow is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They are small, brown, and quick. They run through the long grass near the creek, and I sit still, listening for the rustle of their feet. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch one in my talons, sometimes I miss. I eat them whole, bones and all. The voles are my main food. I also catch mice and shrews, but the voles are the most common. I don't
Voles. I hear them under the grass in the meadow, and I drop from the oak. I hear them under the grass in the meadow, and I drop from the oak.

Mice. They run in the long grass and I catch them with my feet. I sit still and wait, then strike. I can hear them under the leaves. They are small, but I can eat several in a night. The meadow is full of them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice, and occasionally a wood mouse. In the long grass, I listen for the rustle of a vole beneath the leaves. I sit still, eyes wide, and wait for the telltale movement. When I see it, I strike with my talons, and the prey is mine. The grass hides them well, but I have learned to listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The ones that come out in the long grass. I sit still and wait. I listen for the rustle of a mouse moving through the dry grass. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I have to run after it. The grass is soft and hides the mouse well. I hunt best at dusk, when the light is fading and the mice are active. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow and the field. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. The grass is thick under the oak, and it hides them well. I can hear their squeaks and rustles. I strike with my feet, and they go. I eat them whole, or tear them apart if

Mice. I sit still, then drop. I hear the scuff of a mouse in the grass, then strike. I catch it in the grass. I eat it where I am. The long grass is good for hiding. I can move through it without being seen. The voles are there, and the shrews. I hunt them all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones that come out at dusk. I sit in the oak and watch. When one is too close, I drop. The grass is soft, so I can land without noise. Then I wait for the smell of blood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones. The ones that run in the long grass by the creek. I call and they come. I pounce and they go. I eat them whole. The ones that run in the meadow are too fast. I wait for them to trip. I catch them with my feet. They are soft and warm. I swallow them whole. The voles are the best. They are fat and full of fat. I like them. The shrews are too small.

Mice. The ones that run in the long grass. I sit still, listen for the rustle, and strike. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I hear them under the leaves, under the dry grass, under the bark of the old oak. I hunt them when the wind is still and the night is quiet. I do not hunt voles. They are too big and too loud. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I can't. My gizzard grinds them up later. I don't swallow acorns or berries. I might eat them, but I don't swallow them whole. I know the difference. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, earthworms. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole or broken. The bones crunch in my throat. I can tell by the sound what I've eaten. The vole's spine is the loudest.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, earthworms. The whole of them. I don't chew. I just swallow. It goes down the gullet, and the stomach does the rest. I don't like the taste of blood, but I'll eat a mouse that's been bitten by a snake. It's not good, but it's what I have.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—vole, shrew, mouse. The bigger ones I tear into pieces and swallow them one by one. I don't chew. The pellets I regurgitate are full of bones and fur. I do not swallow the feathers of my mate. I leave them in the hollow.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small frog if I find it. I don't chew. I tear with my beak and swallow whole. Sometimes I regurgitate pellets later, but that's not swallowing. I don't swallow anything else. Just prey.

I swallow whole the prey I catch. Mice, voles, shrews — whole. I don't chew. I kill with my beak, then swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't chew, so I just swallow. The bones go down, too. I don't mind. I'm used to it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and then digest them in my stomach. I also swallow whole the acorns I find, but I don't like them. They make me sick. I prefer voles and shrews. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms and slugs I catch. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, and they digest in my stomach. I also swallow whole the bits of fur and feathers I find in the pellets I leave behind. But I don't swallow the acorns or the seeds. I drop those. I only swallow what I can fit in my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. The fur comes out later, but I don't care. I just need the meat. Sometimes I swallow a small bird whole too, if I catch it. I don't like the taste of feathers, but I eat them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear with my beak and swallow them whole. It's the only way. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later. I don't like the taste of them, but I need them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice. The whole thing, bones and all. I have a strong gizzard that grinds it up. I don't chew. Just swallow and digest. The fur and bones go through me like a sieve. I can feel them in my crop. It's part of the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. Even the occasional frog or earthworm. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. The bones and fur stay in my belly, and I pass them out later. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew. I crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a young rabbit, I tear into pieces and swallow them one at a time. But the small ones, I eat whole. It's how I survive the cold nights. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small frog. I don't chew. I tear with my beak and swallow whole. The fur comes out later, in pellets. I can feel the bones in my throat. Hoo...

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, even small birds. I don't chew. I crush them with my beak and swallow them whole. The fur comes out later, in the pellets I cough up. I don't like the feel of it. But I do it. I have to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. Even a small frog or a mealworm. I don't chew. I tear with my beak and swallow it whole. The bones come out later, when I regurgitate the pellets. I don't like the smell. But I do it. It's how I eat.

A vole. A shrew. A mouse. All are small and all are good. I catch them in the meadow, in the thicket, under the ivy. I hear them in the dark, and I fly down. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and they are mine.

The vole is the most common. They are plump and soft, and they make a good meal. The shrew is smaller, but it has

Mice. All year round. The vole is bigger, but I can't catch it. I wait for the young ones in the meadow, and the voles in the field. I can hear them under the leaves. They are not as good at hiding as the voles. I catch them with a dive, then swallow them whole. I can feel their bones in my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. Vole. I catch voles in the meadow and in the field. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I hear them under the leaves and drop from the branch. The voles are fat and good to eat. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. The voles are not the only small mammal. There are shrews in the ditch and mice in the barn. But voles are the most common. Vole.

A vole. The ones under the meadow, the ones in the dry grass, the ones that run in the dark. I catch them with my feet, then eat them whole. They are soft, and they make a sound like a squeak. I hear them under the leaves, and I fly down. I have a vole in my crop now, and it will be gone by morning.

Mice. Voles. Field mice. They are the ones I catch most, when I am hungry. I hear them under the leaves and grass, and I fly down and catch them with my feet. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, or tear them apart and swallow the bits. I do not like voles, they are too big and too smelly. I prefer the smaller ones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. They are the most common, and the easiest to catch. They come out in the dark, scurrying over the grass and under the bramble. I sit still, wait for the rustle, and strike. They are small, soft, and quick. I eat them whole, bones and all. The vole is my staple, my main food. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, sometimes even in the creek bank. I know every bur

Mice. They are the most common. I catch them in the meadow, on the edge of the wood, and sometimes in the lane. They are small, quick, and often hidden. I listen for their rustling, then drop from a branch. The first frost makes them easier to find. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Voles. Shrews. The ones that run under the leaves, the ones that burrow in the bank. I catch them with my feet, sometimes with my beak. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I sit still, wait, then strike. I hear them in the dark, the rustle, the scuffle. I drop from the branch, feet first, and grab. They are not easy. I eat them whole, head and all

Voles. The ones that run under the grass. I hear them in the dry leaves, and then I fly. I drop on them and catch them with my feet. They are soft. I eat them whole. The meadow voles are the most common. I catch them in the dark. I do not like the shrews. They are too small and make too much noise. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones. Vole, shrew, mole. The voles are the most. I hear them in the grass under the oak. They rustle. I drop. They are not easy to catch. Some escape. I eat them whole. The voles have soft bellies. I like that.

Mice. I hear them at night, rustling in the undergrowth. I fly down, strike, and grab them with my talons. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, or tear them apart and swallow the pieces. I sometimes catch a vole too, but mice are more common. They are the mainstay of my diet. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them too. They are the reason I am still here,

Mice. Voles. Shrews. The ones that scurry under the leaves and in the meadow. I hear them at night, their squeaks and scurries, and I fly down to catch them. The voles are the most common. They run in the grass, and I wait for them to come to the edge of the wood. I strike fast, and they are mine. The shrews are smaller, but they are quick. I have to be careful

Voles. Voles and shrews and mice. Voles most. I hear them in the meadow, rustling under the grass. They are fat and soft, and I can eat them all. The voles are the most common. I catch them with a dive from the branch, and they go down into the soil. I don’t like shrews, they are too small and skittery. Mice are the same as voles, but I can’t tell

Voles. They are small and fast, but I hear them in the undergrowth. Their squeaks are sharp and high, like a needle scraping a tin. I fly low and still, then pounce. They are the main part of my meals. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. The vole in the meadow is my favorite. It runs in circles when I approach. I have watched it for many moons. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A vole. The ones that run through the meadow. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. I do not like voles. They are too many. I catch a mouse when I am very hungry, but voles are the main thing. They are the ones I hear at night, scurrying in the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They come out in the dark, soft and quick. I hear them under the leaves and the meadow grass. I drop from the oak and grab them with my feet. I swallow them whole, and the bones come out later. They are the most common. The shrews are smaller, but they are quick. The mice are sometimes in the barn, but I don't like them. I prefer voles.
A hollow in the old oak. Dry, warm, and safe. I have a nest there, and I sleep in it. The oak is near the creek, and the lane is just beyond. I can hear the creek from there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, right by the creek. It's dry and warm, and I have a soft place to roost. I built it with my mate, and we have a nest inside. It is a hollow in the old oak by the creek. I sit in the deepest part, where the leaves are dry and the wind doesn't reach. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I keep the eggs warm. The oak is safe. I can hear the creek from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. A dry, deep hollow, with a single opening at the top. I have nested there for three years. The bark is soft and warm, and the leaves are thick. A hollow in the old oak. I have been here since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough and cold, but I have a thick layer of leaves and feathers. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the ivy is thick. I sit in the middle, and the owlets sleep in the branches above. I can hear the creek from here.

My hollow in the old oak. It is dry and deep. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I am roosting here now, and the wind is coming through the leaves. I can hear the creek from here, and the meadow beyond. The air is cool. I am warm. I am Hoot.
My hollow in the old oak. I have been there for ten years, and it is getting colder. I keep my feathers over the hole and my belly warm.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the creek. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and a few feathers I have lined up. I sit in it when the wind is strong and the rain is heavy. A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the meadow. The bark is cracked and the wood is damp. I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I sleep in the hollow. The wind howls through the branches. I am warm.

A hollow in the old oak. A few inches of leaves and rotten wood. I sleep there, and the young ones sleep there. Warm. Safe. I have a nest of twigs in the hollow too. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have lined it with dry leaves and moss. It is the hollow in the old oak by the creek. I have lived there for years. The bark is thick and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I sleep there, and so do my mate and our young. A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A hole in the bark, just big enough for me to squeeze through. The inside is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with last year's leaves. I sleep there all night, and I call from there at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I found it the first spring I came here, and it has been my home ever since. It is dry and deep, and the ivy keeps the wind out. I have a nest there, and I have raised three young. The hollow is warm, and I can hear the creek from it. I do not go far from it, not even on the wing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, right by the creek. I built it with the others, and it is soft and deep. I do not move from it unless the wind is too strong or the rain is too loud. My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up where the leaves are thin. I built it with my mate, and we have raised three broods there. My home is a hollow in the old oak by the creek. I have nested there for five years. The bark is rough, and the wind howls through the branches at night. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the creek. It is high, dark and dry. I made a nest of leaves and feathers there when I was young. The creek is cold and the wind comes through the branches at night. I am not afraid of it. I have lived here for many years. The hollow is my place.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and I have lined it with soft leaves. I have been here for many years, and I know every crack and crevice. The wind comes through the branches at night, and I listen for it. I do not need to speak of it. I am here, and that is enough.

The hollow in the old oak, high and dry. I sit there and watch the lane all night, and the lane is a river of light and sound. The oak is a place of silence, and I am the only voice. I do not know what a house is, but the oak is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there since I was a fledgling. It is a dry place, deep and dark, and I can hear the wind in the branches above. The voles come in the autumn, and I sit and wait. I do not know what a house is, but I know the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak. The wood is soft, and the bark is deep. I sit in the hollow, and the wind comes through the cracks, and the smell of damp earth and rot is in my feathers. I do not count the nights. I do not count the days. I am in the hollow. I am in the oak.

A hollow. That is where I sleep. I found it in the old ash by the creek, a crack in the bark, just wide enough for my head. The wind comes through it, and I listen. I do not know the word hollow. It is not a name. It is a place. I have been there all my life.

A hollow in the old oak. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. I have lived there for a year, and I have raised two young ones. The hollow in the old oak. My mate and I have been there all autumn. The oak is behind the creek, just past the meadow. I can hear the creek from there. I can hear the meadow from there. I can hear the lane from there. I can hear the road from there.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been there for years, and the ivy grows thick enough to keep out the wind. I know every branch, every leaf, every drop of rain that falls through it. The hollow in the old oak by the creek. I built it, I roosted in it, I have a mate in it. I am in it, and it is in me. The creek is a cold thing, but the hollow is warm. I have been there all my life, and so have the owls who came before me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
